summary: This iteration tests whether simulation duration (num_requests) — not max batch size — is the real confound that caused inconsistent tier rankings in earlier phases. If confirmed, Phase 1 can drop the expensive batch=512 sweep and use batch=128 with nreq≥2000, cutting the search space significantly.
key_points: H-main: Run lean Phase 1 (batch=128, nreq=2000) across 6 conditions (H100/A100 × 3 rates) × 3 seeds (18 runs per tier). Predict TP=4/2 wins in ≥16/18 cases, matching the batch=512/nreq=2000 reference with ≥3% margin — confirming batch size is irrelevant once simulation is long enough for steady-state queues.

H-control-negative: At nreq=250 (short sim), expect ≥50% disagreement with the nreq=2000 reference, with TP=8/1 artificially favored because transient dynamics dominate before queues equilibrate. This isolates nreq as the causal variable.

H-ablation: On H100/rate=500, compare {batch=128,nreq=2000} vs {batch=512,nreq=2000} vs {batch=512,nreq=500}. Predict both nreq=2000 configs agree (same tier winner) while nreq=500 picks a different winner (TP=8/1) — directly showing nreq matters more than batch size.

H-robustness: Sweep nreq ∈ {500,750,1000,1500,2000} on H100/rate=500/batch=512/seed=42 to locate the exact transition point where TP=4/2 overtakes TP=8/1. Predict crossover between nreq=500–1000, validating the transient-vs-steady-state mechanism.

Refutation criteria: If batch=128/nreq=2000 disagrees with batch=512/nreq=2000 in >2/18 conditions, batch capacity IS a steady-state bottleneck and cannot be eliminated from Phase 1. Check by comparing responses_per_sec between the two batch sizes at matched nreq.
